title: CMPC to sell Chilean forestland to J.P. Morgan Natural Capital for $365.5 million - Lesprom Network
content: Empresas CMPC SA , Forestal Mininco SpA., J.P. Morgan, J.P. Morgan Natural Capital Chilean forest products company Empresas CMPC has agreed to sell about 60,000 hectares of forestland in the Maule region, mainly radiata pine plantations, to Bosques San Pedro, part of J.P. Morgan Natural Capital, for $365.5 million, the company said. The assets account for almost 5% of CMPC's total forestland. Subsidiary Forestal Mininco signed the asset purchase agreement on Wednesday. Part of the price, which is subject to customary adjustments, will be paid at closing and the rest as the properties are registered to the buyer, which is expected within the next three months. The deal includes a long-term wood supply agreement under which CMPC will buy timber from the sold plantations for its paperboard mill in Maule. CMPC expects the sale to have a positive effect on its results in the fourth quarter of 2026 and the first quarter of 2027, but the amount cannot yet be determined. title: J.P. Morgan Asset Management Raised Its Long-Term Hedge Fund Return Forecast to 6.7%: - HedgeCo.Net
content: HedgeCo.Net — J.P. Morgan Asset Management has raised its 10-to-15-year return forecast for diversified hedge funds to 6.7% from 5.3%, a 140-basis-point increase, in its 2027 Long-Term Capital Market Assumptions. The firm attributed the upgrade to higher alpha estimates and higher interest rates, and Hedgeweek reported it was the largest upgrade to any alternative asset class in the report. The 31st edition of the assumptions, which cover more than 200 assets in more than 20 base currencies, puts alternatives at the center of portfolio construction. J.P. Morgan projects a 7.0% annual return for a U.S. dollar 60/40 stock-bond portfolio, but said higher stock-bond correlations call for more diversification. A portfolio with 30% in diversified alternatives lifts the projected return to 7.5% and improves the Sharpe ratio by 21% compared with a simple 60/40 mix, the firm said. Across private markets, the forecasts moved in different directions. The private equity assumption slipped slightly to 9.8%, with returns tied to repeatable operational value creation, including AI use in portfolio companies. Global core infrastructure rose to 7.1% from 6.5%, helped by expected gains for transportation assets as manufacturing reshores, while U.S. core real estate eased slightly to 8.1% and European core real estate rose to 7.1%. The report also introduced a return range for bitcoin for the first time but did not include it as an allocation. “With dispersion wider than it has been in years, investors anchored to a disciplined strategic asset allocation will find this a more compelling environment than the headlines suggest,” said Grace Peters, global co-head of investment strategy for J.P. Morgan Private Bank. John Bilton, global head of strategic research for multi-asset solutions, said the outlook combines higher global bond yields with alternatives and real assets for differentiated returns and inflation resilience. For hedge fund allocators, the important detail is the source of the upgrade. Because the higher forecast rests largely on alpha rather than market beta, as Hedgeweek noted, it depends on manager selection, and the report stresses that its assumptions are passive and do not reflect fees or implementation costs. Still, a major house raising its long-run hedge fund estimate by more than any other alternative asset class gives consultants and CIOs a new reference point heading into 2027 planning. title: JPMorgan warns the K-shaped US economy could spark a broader macro shock - Yahoo Finance UK
content: Tip: Try a valid symbol or a specific company name for relevant results The K-shaped recovery risks sparking a new economic shock, JPMorgan Asset Management says. The bank outlined several risks that stemmed from the widening gap between high and low earners. The K-shaped economy will likely persist, it said, citing expectations of higher capital gains. America's K-shaped economy is sticking around, and it could what sparks a fresh economic shock, JPMorgan Asset Management is warning. In a recent report, the bank's asset management arm highlighted fragilities associated with the K-shaped economy, in which lower-earning households struggle while higher-earning Americans do fine. The bad news: The K-shaped divergence doesn't look like it's going to even out anytime soon. What's more, the split in the economy could also be a catalyst for macro and market volatility, a team led by George Gatch, the CEO of the asset manager, wrote in a report. The bank pointed to how capital gains are poised to grow faster than income from labor in the coming years, a dynamic that should keep economy K-shaped. US stock investors are sitting on a tidy nest egg after years of bull market euphoria, but most of the US's stock wealth is concentrated among the upper percentiles of earners. The S&P 500 is up 70% in five years. Additionally, households in the topmost income quintile are sitting on $56.3 trillion in stock and mutual fund wealth, or 87% of all household stock and mutual fund wealth in the second quarter, according to the latest Fed data. The bank said it expects growth in US large-cap stocks to clock in at around 7.5% a year. Meanwhile, labor productivity growth from AI is expected to be far more subdued, with JPMorgan estimating that AI could boost US total factor productivity growth to around 1.2% annually in its base case. It's also unclear how the productivity gains from AI will be distributed among lower- and middle-income Americans, who make up the lower leg of the K-shaped economy. The bank highlighted several risk scenarios to the economic outlook if the needs and distribution of resources in the K-shaped economy were to shift. In one scenario, workers demand more resources than economists currently expect, potentially destabilizing the broader economic and financial ecosystem. In another, the US attempts to redistribute the capital returns from AI, which inadvertently disincentivizes investment, producing a string of knock-on effects. Alternatively, the US is also at risk of "widespread capital misallocation," and if the investment boom fails to meaningfully boost US productivity, economic growth could trend lower, the report added. "A K-shaped economy, with unequal returns to capital vs. labor, is a metastable state — surprisingly durable, but sensitive to stress or shock," the bank wrote, adding that a miscalculation of balances between the upper- and lower-legs of the K-shaped economy was the "greatest risk" to its economic outlook. "While we expect the metastable equilibrium of the K-shaped economy to persist, factors that push the balance of rewards between capital and labor too far in either direction could cause bouts of volatility," it added. The K-shaped economy has been part of the zeitgeist in recent years, particularly as the post-pandemic AI-boom has minted wealth for asset owners, while people who don't own stocks are left out. But there are signs that even higher-earning Americans are starting to pull back on spending, a signal that even the upper-leg of the K-shaped economy may be feeling the pain of hotter inflation and high gas prices. JP Morgan has reiterated its 'overweight' rating on ConvaTec Group PLC (LSE:CTEC), saying the medical products group is well positioned to meet its 2026 earnings guidance and that its 2027 outlook is increasingly secure ahead of a trading update next month. A research note ahead of ConvaTec’s 10-month trading update on 18 November said the bank had made changes to its divisional growth mix for the second half, while leaving group forecasts largely unchanged. Housekeeping changes to items below operating profit increased JP Morgan’s earnings per share forecasts by 7.9%, putting its estimates about 2% above consensus for 2026 and 1% ahead for 2027. The broker said management had reiterated confidence in the second-half improvement needed to meet full-year guidance, with growth expected to accelerate from 21.2% in the first half to about 25% in the second half. The anticipated improvement includes a more favourable product mix, the timing of orders in the advanced wound care division and cost efficiencies, factors JP Morgan considers to be within management’s control. Concerns about whether Convatec can deliver the required second-half acceleration have weighed on its shares, but the bank believes reaffirmation of full-year guidance at the November update could ease investor doubts. JP Morgan also sees an attractive valuation relative to Danish medical equipment maker Coloplast, highlighting a potential long Convatec, short Coloplast trade. Convatec trades at 13.8 times forecast earnings for 2027 and 12.1 times for 2028, compared with Coloplast’s respective multiples of 18.3 and 16.7 times. The broker expects Convatec to deliver double-digit earnings growth, while warning that Coloplast could face a weak first-quarter performance in its 2027 financial year and cuts to its medium-term forecasts. JP Morgan said the relative valuation gap makes the pair trade compelling, given its view that Convatec’s guidance risks have diminished while uncertainty around Coloplast’s outlook remains elevated. title: Could the 10-Year Treasury yield reach 5.75% in 2027? Here's what our JPMorgan strategists think - Chase Bank

The bond market has a reputation for being the stock market’s sleepier counterpart, but a rapid rise in Treasury yields has likely woken up a lot of investors. The yield on a 10-year U.S. Treasury note (a benchmark for government bonds) climbed to 5.35% intraday on October 7, a level not seen since 2002.  Footnote 1 Opens overlay   The swell had been building steadily for months, but a 50-basis-point jump in September was among the top 10% of monthly moves since 1962.  Footnote 2 Opens overlay “In a world of 5.00% nominal growth, it is perfectly normal for the 10-year Treasury yield to be hovering around that level,” J.P. Morgan Wealth Management’s Chief Global Investment Strategist Phil Camporeale said. When the 10-year yield moves that much, it can ripple through the economy: Bond prices can swing, borrowing costs can shift, and markets can reprice expectations for growth and inflation. “The rise in rates has been getting a lot of attention, but investors should remember that a trademark of this post-pandemic cycle has been the lack of sensitivity of both the stock market as well as the broader economy to higher rates,” Camporeale said. So, what comes next? Could yields go even higher? It’s impossible to predict, but our strategists at J.P. Morgan Wealth Management say investors should be prepared for elevated yields to stick around. Instead of guessing at a single data point, our Global Investment Strategy team forecasts a yield range under three potential scenarios. As of October 2026, our strategists' base case for mid-2027 is a 10-year Treasury yield of 5.00% to 5.50%. In this scenario, yields largely stabilize and remain elevated, but they don’t necessarily rise or fall far. Could the 10-year Treasury yield instead climb to 5.75%? It’s possible. For example, if the average price of diesel – which hit a record over $6.50 a gallon in September (compared with $3.50 when the war with Iran began), according to AAA – rose to $10 or more and remained there, the U.S. economy would likely suffer significant strain and rising costs.  Footnote 3 Opens overlay   That’s a component of our strategists' bear case, in which 10-year Treasury yields rise to 5.50% to 6.00%. Then there’s the bull case, in which yields recede to a range of 4.25% to 4.75%. This would become more plausible if the Federal Reserve’s presently hawkish monetary policy cycle does cool inflation and economic growth.  Footnote 4 Opens overlay It's important to note that the 10-year yield tends to peak around the final rate hike of a tightening cycle. Our strategists expect two additional rate hikes of 25 basis points in the current cycle (50 basis points in total), though they do not anticipate a move at the October Federal Open Market Committee meeting. At a high level, the 10-year Treasury yield is influenced by three big forces: Fed policy, inflation and economic growth, and how much extra compensation investors demand to hold a 10-year bond. When investors expect the Fed to raise interest rates, or stay hawkish for longer, yields tend to rise. When the market anticipates rate cuts, yields often fall. Then there’s inflation and growth. High inflation can eat into or entirely outpace the nominal return from a fixed-income bond. Meanwhile, a surging stock market can make bonds look unattractive. In periods of high inflation and strong stock market performance, investors often require higher yields to feel secure enough to buy Treasuries. Conversely, if inflation holds steady near the Fed’s 2% target or growth stalls, yields tend to fall. When the price of diesel goes up, businesses that rely on diesel (such as trucking, freight and agriculture) often pass on their higher costs to consumers. That inflationary pressure could push Treasury yields higher. Demand for Treasuries can also affect yields. When people rush to buy Treasury notes, the yield tends to fall. Case in point: After the 10-year yield hit its highest level in more than two decades in October, the government auctioned $39 billion in 10-year notes. Yields receded in the days that followed.  Footnote 5 Opens overlay A Treasury security with a high yield, backed by the full faith and credit of the U.S. government, can be an attractive investment for those looking to hedge against stock market risk. Higher Treasury yields tend to drive broader bond market yields higher, too. If yields rise for Treasuries, which are considered a safe fixed-income investment, other bonds with different risk profiles also begin to offer investors higher yields, including relatively low-risk corporate bonds. Our strategists note that elevated yields could make high-quality bonds a timely consideration as part of a diversified portfolio. But that isn’t the whole story, as higher yields can impact your financial life beyond your investment portfolio. When it costs the federal government and businesses more to borrow funds, it tends to cost consumers more, too. Rising rates on mortgages and personal loans often move alongside higher Treasury yields. A historic growth cycle driven by artificial intelligence investment and an energy shock driven by geopolitical conflict have created a macroeconomic environment where the bear case and the bull case both seem plausible depending on how things play out from here. Because market conditions can change, consider using these scenarios as a framework for a portfolio conversation with a financial professional. You may want to focus on how much interest rate risk you’re comfortable with, what role high-quality fixed income plays in your plan, and how you’d want the portfolio to behave if yields move toward the bull or bear case. title: Goldman Sachs, JPMorgan and Morgan Stanley are dominating the AI stock boom. Here's their edge - CNBC
content: Fueled by the global boom in artificial intelligence stocks, relaxed capital rules and greater lending to hedge funds, big Wall Street banks have already had a banner year for equities trading — even with one quarter left to go. The five biggest investment banks have generated about $67 billion in equities revenue through Sept. 30, according to company filings. That is $7 billion more than what the group made during all of 2025, which itself was a record haul. But it's Wall Street's Big Three that have captured the largest slice of what is shaping up to be the industry's most lucrative arena: Goldman Sachs, JPMorgan Chase and Morgan Stanley have made a combined $52 billion in stock trading revenue so far this year, nearly 80% of the total. "When it comes to the AI mega trade, the Big Three consider each other their main competitors, and that's pretty much it," Mike Mayo, Wells Fargo banking analyst, told CNBC. "They've been best positioned to take advantage of this market." Wall Street banks are experiencing an epic run of blockbuster profits as the total value of the stock market balloons and trading activity from institutional and retail investors rises across stocks, exchange-traded funds and derivatives. Helping drive this activity are the loans that the banks, through their prime brokerages, are extending to hedge funds so that they can amplify their bets. Prime brokerage — the business of providing hedge funds with margin loans, securities lending and other trading services — has become a key battleground and source of growth. The Big Three's prime brokers are central to the larger equities story because they serve the largest funds across markets and products. Demand for leverage to make bets on AI hardware, hyperscalers and chip suppliers has reached new heights, bank executives said last week. At Goldman Sachs, equities financing activities jumped 96% in the third quarter to a record $3.37 billion. JPMorgan and Morgan Stanley don't break out that figure, but said they saw a similar dynamic. "I like your 'insatiable demand for capital' point. That feels about right," JPMorgan CFO Jeremy Barnum said on the bank's third-quarter conference call, responding to analyst questions about financing demands. "In this moment where AI is such an overwhelming theme ... there is capital being tapped through all kinds of different mechanisms," Barnum said. That demand has helped transform equity desks at the Big Three from cyclical, transactional businesses into more durable, high-margin lending engines, Wall Street executives say. The performance gap between Wall Street's giants and rivals including Bank of America and Citigroup highlights a widening divide in capital markets. "For clients, the value isn't just a price on one trade, it's coverage and continuity," Rachid Alaoui, JPMorgan global head of equities, told CNBC in an interview. "You want a dealer that can give you the full suite across products, and you want that service to travel with you across regions. That matters in stressed markets and periods of volatility." Executing multibillion-dollar bets, like leveraged swaps on volatile AI stocks or sector ETFs, can require an enormous balance sheet. The biggest banks can absorb potential $100 million losses without threatening their quarters, according to trading executives. Smaller or more niche banks can't underwrite single-trade risks of that magnitude, forcing them to decline the business or cede share. U.S. prime brokers have also benefited from the retreat of European banks including Credit Suisse from the equities business, said Bloomberg Intelligence analyst Herman Chan. "Prime is one of the ultimate scale businesses," Chan said. "If you have a strong equities franchise, the hedge funds will want to transact with you because you have a bigger pool of trading opportunities with counterparties." While U.S. markets were swept up in software and cloud computing giants this year, trading executives say the fastest-growing frontier for equities was in Asia. Institutional investors poured into South Korea and Taiwan, targeting the "picks and shovels" of the AI supply chain: the memory chipmakers and semiconductor manufacturers supporting data center construction, Alaoui said. For the Big Three, with their footprints across Tokyo; Hong Kong; Seoul, South Korea; and Mumbai, India; the Asia trade was a goldmine. However, trading executives point out that transaction taxes and stamp duties are included in top-line revenue, artificially inflating Asia prime totals. There is also no agreed-upon definition of what equities trading revenue should include, so some banks include business lines like clearing services that others exclude from their stock trading totals, making apples-to-apples comparisons difficult. But that doesn't change the overall momentum of the business, boosted by a stock rally that began in October 2022, weeks before OpenAI released ChatGPT. "We're still in a stock-based world," Morgan Stanley CEO Ted Pick said on the firm's earnings call. "Equities are still, all things being equal, the attractive asset class." While the CEOs of Goldman Sachs and Morgan Stanley have said the AI build-out is still in its early years, if AI turns out to be not as transformative as hoped, a downturn could impact those banks more than others, analysts said. The boom has also drawn some concern over the possible risks posed by hedge funds. The International Monetary Fund warned this month that growing leverage, crowded positions and correlated selling from hedge funds could create potential stability risks. The IMF estimated that global hedge fund assets had reached $13 trillion. In August, JPMorgan CEO Jamie Dimon said industrywide leverage was "the highest it's ever been," though he stopped short of calling the risk big enough to pose a threat to the financial markets. Wall Street executives and analysts pointed out that the industry wasn't fazed by the meltdown of several hedge funds this summer. While the hedge fund run by former OpenAI researcher Leopold Aschenbrenner, Situational Awareness, garnered the most headlines, several smaller firms also experienced a forced unwinding. Prime brokers have learned to leap on margin calls and quickly take down risk when markets move against clients, JPMorgan's Alaoui said. "In the summer, some investors had positions they were forced to unwind," he told CNBC. "They deleveraged, risk came down, and the market moved on." Another factor driving the equities boom: Trump administration regulators have eased some leverage rules for the largest U.S. banks, giving them more room to expand balance sheet-heavy businesses including prime brokerage. The revised rules were finalized in 2025, and banks were allowed to adopt them as early as January. By easing the stringent balance sheet caps that previously treated Treasurys and prime brokerage loans, which are collateralized, the same as riskier assets, regulators gave dealers greater flexibility to deploy balance sheet capital. "Capital did go down, so you have to say the system is somewhat more levered because of the relaxation in regulations," said Darrell Duffie, a finance professor at Stanford University and a leading expert on financial stability. "It's not a good idea, but it hasn't gotten dramatically out of whack." The larger size of the market and higher volatility can create more trading, derivatives activity and leverage, he said, but that's not inherently alarming. Wall Street executives also downplayed concerns over leverage, pointing out that they use collateral and frequent stress testing to get ahead of problems. "Hedge fund leverage as a contributor of risk to the system is very much in the category of known unknowns," JPMorgan's Barnum said last week. "It doesn't mean it's riskless, but we kind of know what it is." — CNBC's Leslie Picker and Ritika Shah contributed to this report. © 2026 Versant Media, LLC. The projection sits in the firm's 2027 Long-Term Capital Market Assumptions, the 31st edition of an annual report that sets return expectations for more than 200 assets over a 10- to 15-year horizon, using data as of Sept. 30, 2026. The bitcoin section's authors, portfolio manager Sheena Shah and Dennis Cristallo, head of digital asset strategy at JPMorgan's Global Private Bank, wrote that they "do not make a case for bitcoin (BTC) as a diversifier in portfolios due to its unstable market correlations." Based on this convergence in valuations, JPMorgan (JPM.US) issued a report on October 18, 2026, upgrading Intel (INTC.US) from "Underweight" to "Neutral." This adjustment does not signal a shift to a bullish stance; rather, it reflects the view that the years-long bearish trade on Intel (INTC.US) has largely played out, and that risk and reward are now roughly balanced. The core rationale is that, despite structural improvements in the company's fundamentals, the evidence for a rally remains incomplete, and the market must patiently await the confirmation of key inflection points. From the perspectives of business execution and valuation restructuring, Intel (INTC.US) is undergoing a profound shift in its profit pool. In 2Q26, the Data Center and AI Group (DCAI) generated $2.5 billion in operating profit, surpassing the Client Computing Group for the first time and becoming the company's largest source of profit. According to data compiled by Woofun AI, demand for Granite Rapids servers remains extremely tight, with long-term contracts from clients such as Google (GOOGL.US) extending visibility through 2027. Meanwhile, AI‑enabled PCs now account for two-thirds of the client portfolio, driving ASP improvements and portfolio optimization. On the manufacturing side, 18A‑P has entered risk production, 14A is locked into high‑volume production starting in 2028, the 0.9‑micron process design kit was finalized in October, and EMIB‑T advanced packaging backlog orders are ramping up toward 2027. Following the sharp pullback in 2022, Intel (INTC.US) once again faces a pivotal decision; the market will need to patiently assess the results of its transformation. title: JPMorgan sees 10% annual bitcoin returns, topping stocks, bonds and gold over next decade - CoinDesk
content:
JPMorgan’s (JPM) asset management division expects bitcoin BTC$84,459.46 to outperform U.S. stocks, bonds and gold over the next 10 years. The asset manager forecasted a base case of 10% annualized returns for bitcoin over the next 10 years in its 2027 Long-Term Capital Market Assumptions report on Tuesday. The bank also set a bear case of -9.7% and a bull case of 17%. The figure compared to projected 5.6%-6.6% growth in U.S. bonds, 7.5% and 7.7% in U.S. large and small-cap equities respectively and 5.5% in gold. The report marks the first time JPMorgan has put a range on bitcoin returns in its research. The New York based banking group has a complicated history with cryptocurrency, largely due to the association of CEO Jamie Dimon’s widely publicized views of bitcoin. Dimon famously described the world’s largest crypto as a “fraud” in 2017, a skeptical position he has reiterated with somewhat softer verbiage in recent years. JPMorgan Asset Management maintained a cautious view of bitcoin in Tuesday’s report, saying its “volatility and unstable correlation to other asset classes…remain an obstacle to [its] widespread inclusion in portfolios.” Furthermore, JPMorgan does not make a case for bitcoin as a portfolio diversifier, instead viewing it as a “speculative asset and a hedge against monetary easing,” according to comments by portfolio manager Dr Sheena Shah and head of digital asset strategy Dennis Cristallo. “It lacks a strategic role in portfolios other than as a bet on fiat currency expansion or future asset trading on blockchains,” they added. “BTC mostly trades like a high beta risk asset that tracks global money supply growth, but it is sometimes treated as ‘digital gold.’ Unstable correlations with other assets present a modeling hurdle. A further challenge is forecasting an asset whose fundamentals are not cash flows and whose economics may be as much about adoption, regulation and liquidity as technology.” UPDATE (Oct. 20, 13:15 UTC): Updates to specify report is published by JPMorgan Asset Management. title: JP Morgan Lifts Long-Term Capital Market Return Forecast To 7 Per Cent - Family Wealth Report
content:
Tom Burroughes 
 Group Editor

October 20,  2026 Looking through the gloom of geopolitical events, the US bank's asset management arm sets out a relatively upbeat outlook for how major asset classes will perform, suggesting that adding "diversified alternatives" such as private equity can raise risk-adjusted returns. JP Morgan
  Asset Management has raised its forecast annual return for a
  US dollar 60/40 stock-bond portfolio to 7 per cent over the next
  10 to 15 years, up from 6.4 per cent in last year’s edition. The
  report helps shape how the firm and its clients think about asset
  allocation. “Return matters, but it is no longer the whole story,” Grace
  Peters, global co-head of investment strategy at JP Morgan
  Private Bank, said. “With dispersion wider than it has been
  in years, investors anchored to a disciplined strategic asset
  allocation will find this a more compelling environment than the
  headlines suggest.” For a “60/40+” portfolio, where investors put 30 per cent into
  diversified alternatives, the projected return rises to 7.5 per
  cent, with a Sharpe ratio 21 per cent higher than the plain
  60/40. Last year that figure was 6.9 per cent, with a 25 per cent
  Sharpe ratio uplift. (The Sharpe ratio measures the performance
  of an investment such as a security or portfolio compared to a
  risk-free asset, after adjusting for its risk.) The original portfolio, 60/40, funds a 30 per cent diversified
  alternatives allocation roughly pro rata. JP
  Morgan assumes a 40 per cent allocation to ACWI (All-Country
  World Index of equities), 30 per cent allocation to US aggregate
  bonds, and a diversified basket of alternative investments
  composed of global real estate, infrastructure, transport,
  timberland, gold, hedge funds, private equity, and venture
  capital. As a result, the new allocation looks like
  this:40-30-30. Close correlations between stocks and bonds, which have tested
  the wisdom of the 60/40 approach, make further diversification
  necessary, many in the industry have argued. A decade-plus of
  ultra-low interest rates after the 2008 financial crash hit bond
  yields and equity yields, encouraging an inflow into private
  markets because of their illiquidity premium. The Long-Term Capital Market Assumptions report, now in
  its 31st edition, draws on more than 90 portfolio managers,
  economists and analysts. The assumptions cover more than 200
  assets in over 20 base currencies and underpin strategic asset
  allocation across the group, including at JP Morgan Private Bank. In its explanation about the assumptions, JPMAM said: “We center
  the 2027 edition on three forces with durable implications:
  Economic nationalism (governments’ more domestically oriented
  posture); faster diffusion of technological innovation (tech
  adoption) and the reconfiguration of how and where public and
  private funds are deployed (capital rewiring).” JPMAM said the developed world has the strongest growth outlook
  in 15 years. It expects an AI-centered investment cycle extending
  to 2040 to raise total factor productivity by 50 per cent, to 120
  basis points. That pushes its US real GDP growth forecast to 2.1
  per cent and developed world nominal growth to 4.2 per cent.
  Labor and demographic constraints still weigh on long-term
  growth, and the firm expects inflation to remain more volatile,
  citing demographics, large government deficits and geopolitics.
  It frames the outlook around three forces: economic nationalism,
  technology adoption and a shift in public and private capital
  flows driven by rising domestic investment. In equities, the US large cap forecast rises by 80 basis points
  to 7.5 per cent, on profit margins above 15 per cent, though
  elevated starting valuations and concentration remain
  risks. Global equities are projected to return 7.5 per cent in dollar
  terms, up from 7 per cent, helped by continued but slower dollar
  depreciation. Emerging market equities will fall to 7.1 per cent
  as AI and capital expenditure tailwinds normalize. Developed
  market equity projections will overtake emerging markets for the
  first time in the report’s history, the report continued. Higher real yields will lift the global aggregate bond forecast
  to 5.3 per cent, the highest in two decades and up from a low of
  2.1 per cent in 2021. US intermediate Treasuries are expected to
  return 4.6 per cent, up from 4 per cent a year ago. US investment
  grade credit is forecast at 6.1 per cent, reflecting higher
  baseline rates and heavier issuance from hyperscalers. US high
  yield will rise to 6.7 per cent from 6.1 per cent, with a
  fair value spread of 440 basis points. The largest upgrade among alternatives is for diversified hedge
  funds, raised 140 basis points to 6.7 per cent on higher alpha
  estimates and higher rates. The global core infrastructure area will rise to 7.1 per
  cent from 6.5 per cent, supported by manufacturing reshoring.
  Private equity will edge down to 9.8 per cent and US core
  real estate will slip to 8.1 per cent, while European core
  real estate rises to 7.1 per cent from 6.9 per cent. Broad
  commodities will increase to 4.8 per cent; gold is unchanged at
  5.5 per cent and timberland will dip to 6.2 per cent. The report includes a return range for bitcoin for the first time
  but does not include it as an allocation. title: JPMorgan drops JPM Coin on Ethereum with zero retail access - CryptoSlate

JPMorgan made its JPM Coin deposit token available on Ethereum on Oct. 19, giving its institutional clients another public-blockchain route to send and receive dollar deposits. The launch adds Ethereum's main network alongside the token's existing availability on Base. JPMorgan says the expansion puts native cash on the network where institutions already transact with tokenized assets, collateral and counterparties. That includes its own tokenized money-market funds, bringing the bank's payment and investment offerings onto the same public blockchain. JPM Coin, which uses the ticker JPMD, digitally represents a bank deposit. The bank's Ethereum announcement says it supports peer-to-peer transfers between institutional clients in the Ethereum Virtual Machine ecosystem, including Base and Ethereum. Participation remains tied to the bank's institutional client base. A public network does not make the service available to every Ethereum wallet holder, and the announcement includes no retail rollout. The new route broadens where those clients can transact. In November 2025, JPM Coin became available to institutional clients on Base on November 12, after the proof of concept had begun in June 2025. Base is an Ethereum Layer 2 network. The October launch adds the Layer 1 network itself, extending the deposit token's reach within the Ethereum ecosystem. The deposit token joins investment products already on Ethereum. JPMorgan Asset Management launched My OnChain Net Yield Fund, or MONY, on Ethereum on Dec. 15, 2025. The private-placement money market fund is available to qualified investors through Morgan Money, the firm's investment platform. The JPMorgan OnChain Liquidity-Token Money Market Fund, or JLTXX, followed on May 13, 2026. title: JPMorgan Expands JPM Coin to Ethereum for Tokenized Transfers - PaymentsJournal
content: As an early adopter of digital assets, JPMorgan is now positioned to build on its substantial infrastructure. After bringing its USD-backed deposit token, JPM Coin (JPMD), to the Base blockchain last year, the bank is launching the institution-focused token on Ethereum. Despite the “coin” in its name, JPMD is a unit of account for tokenized deposits—not a stablecoin. It represents deposits held at JPMorgan on a public blockchain, allowing institutional clients to make on-chain payments with greater speed and efficiency. Bringing JPMD to Ethereum, one of the most established blockchains, could expand the token’s reach and potential use cases. This expansion highlights the growing distinction between stablecoins and tokenized deposits. While both represent fiat currency in digital form, stablecoins are typically issued by private companies and backed by reserves. Tokenized deposits, by contrast, represent funds held at regulated banks, a key reason major banks have increasingly favored this approach. Several leading U.S. banks, including JPMorgan Chase, are planning to launch their own bank-led tokenized deposit network. Unlike some of its peers, JPMorgan has invested in digital assets for years. At the center of its efforts is Kinexys, one of the first blockchain platforms developed by a financial institution. The platform has evolved to support a range of functions aimed at streamlining global financial services through digital assets, including bank-to-bank transfers and foreign exchange conversions. JPMorgan recently expanded Kinexys’ foreign exchange capabilities. Last year, the bank also launched its first tokenized money-market fund on Ethereum through the platform. According to the Block, Kinexys has facilitated more than $4 trillion in transactions to date, with an average daily transaction volume of $7 billion. As tokenized deposits offer institutions new ways to streamline and automate transfers, their use could continue to grow, especially among firms engaged in foreign exchange and treasury management. Integrating JPM Coin into these transactions could further expand Kinexys’ role in institutional payments and cross-border finance. JPM Coin, which represents dollar deposits at the bank, was technically deployed on the Ethereum mainnet on Monday and is available for institutional clients’ use, the bank said in an emailed statement. The bank chose Ethereum because the blockchain offers more liquidity than rival networks and is already used by institutional clients, Emma Landriault, the head of Kinexys Labs at JPMorgan’s blockchain division Kinexys, said in an interview with Bloomberg, which reported the news earlier. “Issuing JPM Coin first on Base and now on Ethereum is a meaningful step towards providing our institutional clients with multi-chain optionality for moving wholesale money across both the web3 and traditional finance ecosystems,” she said in the emailed statement. Broadening its availability aims to serve crypto firms that want to make blockchain payments and financial firms that need a digital token to settle trades or back tokenized assets, Landriault said. Tokenization is the process of converting real-world assets and financial assets into a digital form that’s recorded and traded on a decentralized ledger. The advantage is speed, including faster settlement of trades, quick movement of money while bypassing delays and frictions involved in traditional rails. Banks have embraced tokenization, but mostly away from public networks. In the U.S., JPMorgan, Citi (C), Bank of America (BAC) and Wells Fargo (WFC), along with more than a dozen other banks, have plans to start a shared network for tokenized deposits. JPMorgan’s private blockchain network, Kinexys, already handles more than $7 billion a day, a small piece in the bank’s $12 trillion a day payments business. Almost $50 billion worth of crypto assets are locked in Ethereum-based applications, according to DeFiLlama. Abroad, JPMorgan is among more than 30 banks that are helping Swift, the interbank messaging service, define the features and governance of its blockchain-based ledger. title: JPMorgan (JPM) CEO Dimon says the US economy is booming - Newsquawk

Commentary of this kind from the head of the largest US bank has historically functioned as a soft macro data point rather than a tradable event: the chief executive of a systemically important lender sees loan demand, payment flows, and credit performance across the economy in real time, and such remarks have on previous occasions been treated as corroboration of the prevailing growth narrative rather than fresh information. The pattern in past episodes is that upbeat CEO rhetoric matters most when it diverges from, or conflicts with, the official data and the central bank's framing; when it merely echoes consensus, the market imprint tends to be negligible beyond a marginal bid in financials. The distinction worth drawing is between a general characterisation, which carries little weight, and specifics on credit quality, capital markets pipelines, or consumer spending, which are the parts of such commentary that have historically moved bank peers and fed into rate-path pricing. The follow-ons of note are whether similar language appears from peer banks during results season and how the remarks sit alongside the lender's own guidance on net interest income and loan loss provisioning. title: Robot factories and hypersonic missiles: JPMorgan Chase's first $5 billion of defense investments - CNBC
content:
JPMorgan Chase has made $5 billion in startup investments in the first year of its U.S. security and resiliency initiative, the company said Monday, a faster-than-expected pace that indicates the bank is finding plentiful opportunities in emerging defense, manufacturing and supply chain firms. The bank, which last year said it would deploy $10 billion into startups over a decade, may expand the program beyond that initial dollar amount, JPMorgan co-President Doug Petno told CNBC in an interview. Todd Combs, the former Berkshire Hathaway executive who leads the JPMorgan group in charge of making startup investments, has “hit the ground running,” Petno said. “He’s done a great job and put us in some really interesting companies,” he added. Most of those investments have yet to be disclosed, but two known stakes seem emblematic of the project’s mission to bolster companies that are needed for a more dangerous and chaotic era of geopolitics. JPMorgan, the biggest U.S. bank by assets, has taken direct stakes in defense-related startups Hadrian and Castelion. Wars in Ukraine and the Middle East, as well as trade disputes with China, have threatened the flow of energy and key components needed for U.S. industries and defense, which spurred JPMorgan CEO Jamie Dimon into creating the initiative a year ago. He put Petno, widely seen as one of two key possible successors, in charge of the overall investment project. Combs, a former board member of the bank, reports directly to Dimon. The scope of the project extends beyond supply chain, defense and manufacturing to include frontier technologies and the pharmaceutical and health-tech industries. “There’s a lot of really interesting companies that have been working to solve some of these problems,” Petno said. These “early venture-stage, advanced manufacturing companies have found ways to build these capabilities in the U.S.” rather than relying on overseas trading partners, he said. In August, the bank helped lead a $1.4 billion funding round for Hadrian, which builds automated factories that make parts for the defense, aerospace and maritime sectors. A California factory run by Hadrian has 10 robots for every human employee, according to the startup’s founder. That month, JPMorgan was also involved in a $1 billion funding round for Castelion, whose flagship product is a relatively low-cost hypersonic missile called Blackbeard. Castelion was founded in late 2022 by a group of former SpaceX engineers. “Our approach is to find generational companies and partner with them for the long term,” Combs said in a statement Monday. “Putting more than $5 billion to work in our first year shows how many exceptional businesses are building in industries that strengthen critical supply chains,” Combs said. JPMorgan making billions of dollars of direct investments in nascent companies is a departure from its usual role as a lender and advisor. Before the defense initiative, the bank had moved away from taking startup stakes, which can be relatively risky bets on unproven technologies. JPMorgan spun off its private equity business, One Equity Partners, more than a decade ago. In its more traditional role, JPMorgan has also financed and facilitated more than $230 billion for industries that support American national interests, according to the bank. That part of its security and resiliency project, meant to hit $1.5 trillion over 10 years, is led by Jay Horine, a former co-head of investment banking. JPMorgan built a team for the project of about three dozen bankers, who are aided by hundreds more across the firm, as it expanded the initiative to Europe and Canada. Its bankers are mapping distribution lines for key products, from submarines and missiles to aircraft, to identify suppliers that may lack the capital or capacity to meet rising demand, according to Petno.
